activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
The Sánchez family's living room was already full by the time Carson arrived with his dad, and Mr. Sánchez pointed at the last two folding chairs like a referee awarding a corner kick. "Twenty minutes to kickoff," Mrs. Sánchez announced, tapping her watch. On the kitchen counter, a bowl of guacamole the size of a hubcap sat beside a cake shaped vaguely like a soccer ball, which Carson suspected was not a legitimate soccer ball by any measure but was definitely legitimate dessert.

Carson's cousin Inés had flown in from Manchester the night before, and she had claimed the best spot on the couch by arriving an hour early, a tactic Carson had to respect. He'd visited her in England two summers ago and still felt a small sting about the time he'd refused to go with her family to a match because he was afraid of the crowds. He'd regretted it ever since, though he'd never said so out loud.

"Everyone grab drinks now," Mr. Sánchez called. "Halftime is not a snack break, it is a battle for the kitchen." He was calibrating the new projector against the wall, adjusting the picture until the pitch looked green instead of soupy gray, stepping back, squinting, stepping forward again. Above the house, wind turned through the great turbine on the hill behind the neighborhood, its blades sweeping slow circles against the sunset.

When the stadium crowd on screen suddenly stood up in a rippling circle, section by section, arms rising like a tide going around the bowl, Carson stood too, out of instinct. "Wave!" he shouted, arms overhead.

Inés laughed without turning her head. "We call that the Mexican wave."

Carson sat back down slowly. "You do?"

"Everybody at home does," she said. "It went around the world at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico. So we name it for Mexico. Nobody in England just says wave."

Carson filed that away like a trading card. He tried it out quietly, testing whether it fit: a whole country's name attached to arms going up in a stadium. He glanced around the room, at Mr. Sánchez and his family, and decided this was about the best possible living room to have learned it in.

The referee blew the whistle. Guacamole bowls passed hand to hand over heads, the cake got cut before anyone had earned it, and when the first shot on goal skimmed the crossbar, the entire room jumped up at once, all together, no ripples at all.

"Now that," Inés said, "is just a scream with standing."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
story:
Victor had eaten a big lunch on purpose, because tonight he was going to try fasting for Yom Kippur at his grandparent's house. He'd never done it before. At home his parents said it wasn't mandatory for kids, but twelve felt old enough to try.

"How long does it actually last?" he asked Grandpa as the sun dropped behind the neighbor's roof.

"About 25 hours," Grandpa said. "From sunset tonight until after nightfall tomorrow."

Victor frowned. "A day is 24 hours. You can't fast more than a day."

"Figure it out," Grandpa said, and went back to slicing apples for tomorrow's break-fast meal, which sat covered on the counter like a test Victor hadn't studied for.

Victor sat by the window and watched the sky. Sunset didn't mean the sun vanishing, he realized. It meant dipping below the roofline. Nightfall came later, when the sky went properly dark and three stars would show. If you started counting at one edge and stopped at the other edge, you got sunset to sunset, plus the extra stretch of evening. He drew it on a napkin: a little sun, a gap, three stars. It worked. Nobody had told him. He'd found it himself.

The twist came at breakfast time the next morning, when he found Grandma in the kitchen holding a glass of juice she hadn't drunk. "When I was your age, I sneaked food every year," she said. "My father pretended not to notice. Now I can't decide if that was mercy or if he should have made me own up to it." She set the glass down, still full.

Victor thought about that through the long afternoon while his stomach complained. He could compromise, drink water quietly, and no one would know. Instead he walked to the window, waited, and counted stars until he found three. Then he called, "It's after nightfall!"

Grandpa came with the apples, and Grandma brought her juice, still full, to the table too.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Aaron's cabin had a craft hour every afternoon, and this week's project was a color wheel. He cut a circle of poster board, divided it into wedges, and started gluing down paint chips: red next to orange, orange next to yellow, all the way around to purple next to red again. When he finished, he spun the wheel on his pencil point like a propeller, and the colors blurred into a pale gray smear. His friend Marcus thought that was the whole point of the project. Aaron wasn't so sure. He kept staring at the order of the wedges and wondering who had first decided that the colors should go around in a circle at all. Somebody must have tried it first, he reasoned, and whoever that was had to make the same choices he was making. Red and green sat directly across from each other on his wheel. That could not be an accident of his own gluing.

He went to the camp's small lodge library, which was one shelf of paperbacks and a box of old encyclopedias. The entry on color was vague, mostly about light and rainbows, but the entry on Isaac Newton sent him to the article on Newton's book Opticks. There it was, plain as a trail marker: in Opticks, first published in 1704, Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel. Aaron read the line twice. The rainbow that came out of a prism was a straight band, but Newton had bent it around so the ends met, which meant every color got a neighbor on both sides. Aaron looked at his own wheel and saw he had done the same thing without knowing it. He wanted to isolate that fact from everything else on the page, so he copied it onto his hand in ballpoint pen.

At dinner he tried it out on Marcus. "Guess who drew the first color wheel," he said.

"A caveman," said Marcus. "Cavemen painted on walls."

"It was Isaac Newton. In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle."

Marcus put down his fork. "The gravity guy? The apple guy drew a rainbow circle?"

"An early form of the color wheel," Aaron said. "It's in the encyclopedia."

That night Aaron wrote a letter home, because his mother was a graphic designer and would want to know. "Dear Mom," he wrote. "Camp is fine. The lake is cold and Marcus fell off the dock twice in one day, once on purpose. I made a color wheel in crafts. Mine is red-orange-yellow-green-blue-purple, in a circle, with red and green opposite each other. I found out Newton did the first version. In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle. So when you fix colors on the computer, you are basically doing what the apple guy did. Send cookies. Aaron." He read it over, decided the dock story made Marcus sound clumsy rather than funny, and changed "twice in one day" to "twice in one hour," which was more accurate and funnier.

The next afternoon Marcus showed up at craft hour with his own poster board circle. He had drawn six wedges in pencil and filled in the first two, and he had put yellow and purple opposite each other. "I changed my mind about the caveman thing," he said. "But I'm not giving Newton the apple. That part's just showing off."

Aaron held his wheel up beside Marcus's half-finished one. "Spin yours when it's done," he said. "It turns gray."

"Mine's going to turn mud brown," Marcus said. "Better colors."

He reached for the red paint chip.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
story:
The bell on the door jangled as Michael pushed into Kim's Corner Store, his math worksheet crushed in his back pocket. He had exactly one dollar, and one problem: he needed the sour straws for movie night with his brother Danny, but he also needed to finish the worksheet before his mother got home. He set the paper on the counter and studied it while Mr. Kim rang up a woman's lottery tickets. Solve for x, then plot the line. His pencil hovered over the equation 2x + 2 = 8, and behind it a half-empty coordinate grid waited like a taunt.

"You look like a boy carrying a heavy dollar," Mr. Kim said when the woman left. Michael exhaled and told him the truth: if he didn't finish, his teacher would write a citation, his third one, and then no movie night, no sour straws, nothing. Mr. Kim tapped the grid with one finger. "What is confusing you?"

"Everything after the solving," Michael admitted. "Like this point, (3, 5). Danny says it means go up three and over five. I say it's the other way. We argued about it at breakfast until the steam off his oatmeal evaporated and Mom made us stop." Mr. Kim didn't answer. Instead he pulled a napkin from behind the register and drew a quick L-shape on it, two lines like a corner of a fence. He marked three points in pencil and slid it across.

"For you, a game," Mr. Kim said. "You tell me where each dot sits." The first dot was three across and five up from the corner. Michael touched it. "So (3, 5) means across three along the horizontal line first, then up five." He tested it against the second dot, at one across and four up, and the rule held. He checked the third dot, at four across and two up, and it held again. It wasn't random; every single point obeyed. Something in his chest loosened. Back on his worksheet, he solved 2x + 2 = 8, got x = 3, then found the line by plugging in other values, plotting each point across first, up or down second, until the dots connected into a straight ramp climbing the grid.

Michael finished the last point just as Danny burst through the door, breathless, holding his own worksheet and a crumpled napkin. "You left your battleship grid on the kitchen table," Danny said. "I checked every shot you called. You won because you were doing across first the whole time, and I was doing up first. I was aiming at your empty water." Michael laughed so hard he had to set his pencil down. Mr. Kim slid the sour straws across the counter anyway, waved off the dollar, and pointed at the napkin. "Bring back the game," he said. "Next time I hide the dots."

story:
Emily had agreed to one thing, a neighborhood cleanup behind the community center, and had somehow ended up in the food bank's cold room instead, sorting a mountain of slightly dented apples. A note was taped to one crate, written in careful blue ink: "From the back rows we never pick. Take whatever you can use." She read it twice. Bizarre, she thought, that a farm would grow apples and then just not pick some of them.

She began to excavate the bottom of the pile, hunting for more notes, and found the same message on three other crates. Same handwriting every time. She lined the notes up on a steel shelf like evidence and stared at them until Mrs. Alvarez, an older volunteer with reading glasses on a chain, wandered over. "What have we got, a trial?" she asked. "Sort of," Emily said. "I'm waiting for the verdict. Why would a farmer leave whole rows unpicked?" Mrs. Alvarez picked up one of the notes and smiled at it the way people smile at something familiar. "My grandmother would have called that gleaning," she said. "It's an ancient practice. The Book of Leviticus, in the Hebrew Bible, tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers." Then she went back to her boxes of macaroni, and that was all she said.

Emily tested the idea the only way she could. When the farmer's truck pulled up that afternoon, she marched over and asked whether he was leaving the edges of his orchard on purpose. He rubbed his neck. "My grandfather did it, so I do it," he said. "Never met the people who end up eating them. First time anybody's asked."

Emily carried his last crate inside, past the shelf where the notes still hung in a row, and set it down in front of a boy waiting with his mother, who took the top apple without a word.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
story:
Raphael stood on the porch of Wei's house with his bike helmet still on, holding a folded map the two of them had drawn that morning. The plan was simple: ride to the market on Elm Street, buy mangoes, and be back before lunch. The problem was that Wei's grandmother, who was visiting from Taipei, had promised to walk them part of the way, and she did not speak much English.

"Her word for left," Wei said, pulling on his sneakers, "is zuǒ. And her word for right is yòu. They don't sound the same, and they don't mean the same." He said each word twice, letting his voice dip and lift in different places, like two different notes on a piano. Raphael tried copying him. Zuǒ came out flat. Yòu came out flat too. Wei laughed, but not in a mean way.

They set off with Grandmother leading, her canvas shopping bag swinging. At the first corner she stopped, pointed left down a shady street, and said, "Zuǒ." Raphael heard it clearly this time, the tone swooping down and up like a bird changing its mind. He turned left. At the next corner she pointed right and said, "Yòu," her voice falling away at the end like the last step of a staircase. He turned right, and the smell of baking bread from the corner shop told him they were close.

Then Grandmother stopped at a fork where both streets looked the same, dry lawns, parked cars, no signs in sight, and said nothing. She only waited, watching them. Wei whispered, "She wants us to ask. In Mandarin."

Raphael remembered last summer, when he had refused to ask a lifeguard where the pool exit was and had wandered the whole building, missing his swim lesson. The humiliation of it still stung when he thought about it, a small corrosive feeling that had nibbled at his pride all afternoon. He was not doing that again. He took a breath. "Zuǒ?" he said, pointing down the left street, trying to make his voice dip and rise the way hers had.

Grandmother's whole face opened like a window. "Zuǒ," she agreed, nodding, and started down the left street. Wei clapped Raphael on the shoulder. The mangoes turned out to be sweet and slightly bruised, and Grandmother let each of them pick one out.

On the ride home, Raphael tried the words again under the sound of the wind. He could not tell yet whether he was getting the tones right, and he decided that tomorrow he would ask Grandmother to disclose her secret, whether she practiced the sounds in her head before saying them, or whether they just came out shaped that way, like water running downhill. When they reached the porch, he hopped off his bike, looked straight at her, and asked, "Zuǒ? Yòu?" She smiled and pointed to the door, and then, slowly, to the left side of the yard.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
story:
Raphael printed the team roster from the school website and taped it to his bedroom wall, mostly so he could glare at it. Twelve names, and his was not one of them. He had missed the cut for the basketball team by what the coach called "a close decision," which is the kind of thing adults say when they don't want to tell you the actual reason.

His older sister Priya came in without knocking, which was her custom. She wanted the tape, because she was making a poster for her debate club tryout, where she planned to argue that the school should fund a robotics team. She was extremely eloquent about it, practicing her opening line in the mirror every night, though Raphael privately thought the mirror was an easy audience.

"You're going to stare at that thing until it apologizes?" she asked.

"I'm counting birthdays," he said. He had found the roster listed everyone's birthdates, which seemed odd until he realized the school had just reused the eligibility form. He wrote the months on paper, one column for the twelve who made it and one for the kids he knew from tryouts who didn't. Ten of the twelve were born in the first half of the year. Most of them were January through June. He was a December kid. So was his friend Marcus, who was cut too, and so was half the gym class that never stood a chance.

"There's a word for this," Priya said, peering at his columns. "I read it for debate research. The relative age effect. Players born early in the selection year get picked more often than ones born late."

"So it's not my free throw."

"I'm not saying that. I'm saying it's not only your free throw."

The next morning Raphael found Coach Ortiz in the gym, restringing a net. He brought his paper of two columns and asked whether the coach would hold a second tryout in spring, after everyone had six more months of growing under their belts. The coach looked at the columns for a long moment, then at Raphael, who was doing his best not to perspire through his shirt.

"Fine," the coach said. "March. Bring Marcus."

Raphael folded the paper into his pocket, and Priya, waiting in the doorway with her poster board, whispered, "Now do robots."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
story:
Everly sat in the plastic chairs outside Ridge Driving School, waiting for her mom to finish her lesson, with five dollars and a list in her pocket. "Milk, small carton, and practice counting the change," her mom had said that morning. "You're ready." Everly wasn't so sure. She had never walked to Halpern's Corner Store alone before, and the crosswalk at Dent Avenue had a light that felt like it took forever to change.

She watched the traffic light transmit its colors to the intersection, red to green to yellow, and counted the seconds between walks. Nine seconds of green man, then blinking. If she started on the first blink, she could make it. She decided to test that on the way, and when the light finally changed, she stepped off briskly and reached the far curb with two blinks to spare. The woman waiting there with a stroller gave her a small smile, and Everly felt her shoulders drop an inch.

At Halpern's, the milk carton had a bright yellow tag: $3.49. Everly counted out three dollars, two quarters, a nickel, and four pennies from the zippered pocket, then paused. That was exactly $3.59, enough to cover the tag with ten cents to spare. She put the money on the counter. The cashier, a teenager with a name tag reading DEV, rang it up and frowned at the screen.

"You're five cents short," Dev said. "It comes to $3.64."

"But the tag says $3.49," Everly said. "I counted twice."

Behind her in line, a woman with a soft accent leaned over gently. "You must be new to this. It's the sales tax. In the United States and Canada, the price on the shelf leaves out the tax, and it gets added at the till. Back home in the UK, the shelf price already includes VAT, so what you see is what you pay." She held up her own basket. "I still get caught out after four years here."

Everly stared at the numbers on the register, doing the math backward. The tax had to be fifteen cents, because $3.49 plus fifteen made $3.64. So the yellow tag was never the whole story; the real price was hiding until the till. "Do they add tax to everything?" she asked.

"Candy too," Dev said, and pointed at the chocolate bars. "Learn that one early."

"I have ten more cents at home," Everly said, her cheeks warming. "I could run back."

Before she could turn, the woman dug in her coin purse and set a nickel on the counter. "For the milk," she said. "My daughter's about your age, and I'd want someone to do the same for her." Dev dropped the nickel in the drawer, and Everly promised herself she would pass it on someday. She took the milk and the receipt, and on the sidewalk she studied the printed lines: subtotal, tax, total. The pattern was there in black and white.

She walked back to the driving school with the cold carton against her arm, and when her mom came out grinning about her parallel parking, Everly held up the receipt. "The shelf price is a lie in this country," she announced. "In the UK it isn't. And I owe a nice lady a nickel."

story:
Hazel's little brother Theo wanted one thing from the science museum, and it was the rubber alligator from the gift shop. Hazel wanted one thing too: to beat the museum's chemistry challenge station, where a voice from a dusty speaker asked, "Was anything new made?"

The station had two screens. One showed time-lapse footage of ice cubes on a stretch of frozen tundra, melting slowly into puddles while caribou wandered past in the background. The other showed an old bicycle chained behind a shed, its handlebars turning orange and flaky over months. "Physical change or chemical change?" the speaker asked. Hazel had to choose. She glanced at the bicycle. She'd seen rust on the dilapidated playground equipment at school, and the rust hadn't been there when the equipment was new. Something that hadn't existed before was on that metal now.

She looked at the ice again. "Nothing new there," she said. "Ice melting into water is still water. It's just a different shape of the same stuff." She pressed PHYSICAL for the tundra screen. The speaker played a happy chime.

"Show-off," said Theo, though he was grinning.

Then she pressed CHEMICAL for the bicycle, and the chime played again. "Two for two," Hazel announced, and did a small victory dance that made a toddler nearby applaud.

"Fine, you're a genius," Theo said. "Can we go to the gift shop now? That alligator is exposing its teeth at me every time we walk by. It's practically begging."

"It's rubber, Theo. It can't beg."

"It can in my heart."

Hazel laughed and pulled him toward the shop. At the door she stopped, pointed at a display of candles, and asked, "Burning. New stuff made or not?"

Theo groaned. "You're going to quiz me the whole ride home, aren't you?"

"Every mile," said Hazel, and she spun the revolving door for him.

story:
Mason slid his tray along the lunch line, barely noticing that the cafeteria lady had given him the nutritious apple he usually ignored. His mind was stuck on science class, where Mr. Okafor had set a bowl of ice on one table and a sealed jar of rusty nails on another. "By Friday," the teacher had said, "tell me which one can go back to what it was, and why."

At the lab table after school, his friend Priya was already there, arms crossed. "I want the demonstration slot," she said. "I've been waiting three weeks to present."

"You can have it," Mason said, "if you help me figure this out first." Some of his old resentment about her beating him on the last quiz faded as she pulled out her notebook.

They melted an ice cube over warm water and watched it refreeze in the freezer across the room. Easy. But the rust? Priya scraped at a nail with her thumbnail and nothing changed. "It's like the rust belongs to it now," she murmured. "But why?"

Mason remembered the school campout in October, sitting by the fire while Dev threw twigs into the flames. Dev had asked why the black logs couldn't be un-burned, and one of the eighth graders had shrugged and said, "Burning is a chemical change. The wood combines with oxygen and turns into ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour. It can't turn back into wood."

The smoke had been going somewhere, Mason realized. The logs weren't just shrinking; they were leaving, transported upward as gas. The ice cube was only changing shape. The wood had become something else entirely.

He wrote a note to Mr. Okafor and left it in the mailbox on the classroom door: "Dear Mr. Okafor, I tested the ice and the rust. Ice goes back and forth, but rusted metal and burned wood don't go back. Where does the burnt part even go? Come watch Friday. Mason."

On Friday, Priya held the torch, Mason held up a charred splinter, and the class leaned in.

"See this?" he said. "It can never be wood again."

story:
Rebecca sat on her bed with her phone balanced on her knees, glaring at the family group chat, "Lopez Family HQ." At dinner she had told everyone that she had forgiven Priya for repeating the thing about her stutter to Maddie Torres, but that she did not want to be best friends again yet, and her brother Marcus had said that made no sense. "You can't forgive somebody and still not hang out with them," he insisted now, typing fast. "That's like saying you ate the cookie but the cookie is still here." Below his message, he was also begging Mom to post his rocket launch video, which kept failing to upload because the file was too big. Rebecca ignored that. She typed: I'm serious. I'm not mad anymore. I just don't want to be #1 best friends again right away. Is that even allowed?

Grandpa answered first, with his usual metalworking joke: "People are like alloys, mija. Strong stuff, mixed together, but the mix can change." Rebecca rolled her eyes, then stopped, because Aunt Jen, who was a school counselor, sent a short reply: "Totally allowed. Forgiving means letting go of the resentment. Reconciling means rebuilding the relationship. They're two different things." Rebecca read it three times. So she had done the first one, dropped the resentment like a heavy backpack, and the second one, rebuilding, was separate. The friendship didn't have to snap back to exactly how it was. It could be rebuilt slowly, or rebuilt differently, or not rebuilt at all, and she could still have forgiven Priya honestly.

She decided to test it. She texted Priya: I'm not mad at you anymore, for real. But I want to sit somewhere else for a while. Not forever maybe. Just a while. Priya replied with a single thumbs up, which in their private language meant "okay, no arguing." Rebecca noticed she felt lighter, not cured, but lighter, which seemed like evidence that the two things really were separate. Down in the family chat, Marcus had finally solved his own problem by trimming the video to fifteen seconds; the rocket wobbled, lurched sideways, and knocked over Grandpa's birdbath. "That was feasible," Marcus declared. "The launch, I mean. Not the birdbath."

Grandpa replied, "Come over Saturday, we'll build a better fin." Rebecca smiled at her phone and then, before she could talk herself out of it, she saved Priya's contact back to her favorites list, right below family.

Jessica's problem was that her lab notebook had two columns, and she had put salt water in the wrong one. "Water likes to leave when it's warm," Jessica said. "I'm giving it a chance."

Mrs. Okafor drifted past the windowsill, looked in, looked at Jessica, and raised one eyebrow.

"Physical change," Jessica said. "I moved it to the right column."

Mrs. Okafor picked up the beaker and turned it in the light. "You evaporated it and preserved the evidence. Nice."

Marcus leaned over from the next stool. "So if I dissolve sugar in my tea, that's..."

"Physical," said Jessica. "Don't test that one on the windowsill."

He was already unwrapping a candy.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
The Lorensons' living room was packed before the championship even started, and the air had gone humid from all the people and the popcorn. Carter had the best spot on the floor, right in front of the screen, with his soda balanced on a couch leg. Marcus sat beside him, spinning a basketball on one finger, and Mrs. Lorenson kept shushing everybody every time the announcers talked.

During a timeout in the first half, Marcus frowned at the screen. "Okay, but why do they call it a basket? You score in a hoop. There's no basket anywhere."

"Because there used to be actual baskets," Carter said. "James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, and the goals were peach baskets." He'd read it in a library book over winter break and had never once gotten to use it.

"Peach baskets," Marcus repeated. "Like, for peaches."

Before Carter could answer, the screen went black. So did the lamps, the refrigerator hum, everything. Somebody's little sister shrieked, then laughed, and Mr. Lorenson said, "Not the finals," in a voice like the world had personally insulted him.

"The generator," Mr. Lorenson said from the garage doorway. "There's one in the shed, but it hasn't run since the fall storm. If we can't get it going before halftime ends, we miss the whole third quarter." Halftime was twelve minutes. Carter grabbed a flashlight and followed him out.

The generator was heavy, rust-flecked, and stubborn. Mr. Lorenson yanked the starter cord four times with no luck. "Fuel's fine," he muttered, checking the tank. He pulled again. Nothing. His mind flashed back to October, to the day his grandfather had driven four hours through snowy tundra to watch Colton's first math meet and had seen him freeze at the fractions round. "Time," Mrs. Okafor called.

Wyatt cracked three eggs into the cast iron pan and watched the bacon grease shimmer. Dad had hiked down to the creek to fill the water jugs, which meant breakfast was Wyatt's job for the first time, and he intended to elaborate on the usual camp menu with fried eggs and sliced potatoes instead of just oatmeal. His little sister Daisy crouched by the fire pit, already spearing marshmallows onto sticks, because her one ambition for the whole trip was to roast dessert over real flames.

"You can't start those yet," Wyatt said. "Dessert comes after breakfast."

"That's why I'm practicing," Daisy said, holding up a stick. "You practice too. With your eggs."

He turned back to the camp stove just as a tongue of flame jumped from the pan. The bacon grease had caught. Wyatt's hand went straight for the kettle, since water was what you threw at a fire, and then he stopped, because he remembered the lake trip in June. Dad had been frying sausages when the pan flared exactly like this, and instead of reaching for water Dad had said, "Never pour water on a grease fire. Water flashes into vapor and throws the burning oil everywhere," and slid a lid over the pan and shut off the heat, and the fire had gone out, just like that.

Wyatt set the kettle down. He grabbed the pan's lid, but he did not slap it on right away. He watched the flame for half a second and thought it through. The fire was in the oil, not the stove, so turning off the burner would not be enough on its own. And the flame was feeding on air above the pan, which meant a lid ought to starve it. It was the most probable fix he had, and it was the one Dad had used. He turned the knob to off, then slid the lid sideways over the pan the same way he had seen it done, careful to keep his fingers clear.

The flame shrank to a ring, then to nothing. Under the lid, the oil ticked softly as it cooled.

Daisy had gone completely still, marshmallow stick in the air. "Is it out?"

"It's out," Wyatt said. He lifted the lid a crack, saw no flame, and closed it again to let things cool. "Grease fire. You never put water on it, or it throws the burning oil everywhere. You turn off the heat and cover the pan."

"So my marshmallows are safe?" Daisy asked.

"Your marshmallows are safe." Wyatt started a fresh pan, this time with less grease and lower heat, and when Dad came back up the trail with the water jugs, the eggs were already sizzling.

Dad looked at the lidded pan, then at Wyatt. "Everything all right?"

"Had a little flare-up," Wyatt said, and slid an egg onto a plate. "Handled it."

The snow came down like the sky had emptied its whole closet, and Noah found out school was canceled before he even finished his cereal. He whooped so loud his dog, Biscuit, knocked over a chair. By eight o'clock he was bundled in the backyard, where the snow lay lush and deep over the picnic table and the swing set wore a white hat. He was about to nominate Biscuit for the job of first sled rider when his mom called from the porch, "Check the weather before you stay out too long!"

He pulled off one glove and tapped his phone. The screen said twenty-eight degrees, which didn't seem bad at all. But underneath it said "feels like 14." Fourteen! He stared at the two numbers. Same air, same morning, and the phone claimed it felt fourteen whole degrees colder than it actually was. The wind gusted across the yard and the cartilage in his ears stung so hard he grabbed them with both mittened hands, and he thought, okay, maybe. But how could moving air be colder than the air itself? That made no sense.

He decided to test it. First he stood behind the shed, out of the wind, and counted to sixty. Cold, sure, but bearable, like standing inside a refrigerator. Then he marched to the middle of the yard where the flag rope slapped against the pole and the wind came straight at him, and counted to sixty again. Within thirty seconds his cheeks burned and his eyes watered, and Biscuit's ears flattened back like he was being scolded. Same temperature, Noah thought, but it felt completely different out here. The wind had to be the difference.

He tried it once more with his bare hand, holding it still behind the shed and then in the open wind, and the windy side went numb first, every time. So the moving air was doing something the still air wasn't. He remembered the word from the screen and said it out loud. "Wind chill. That's the wind chill."

He ran inside, cheeks blazing, and found his mom at the counter. "The phone says it's twenty-eight but it feels like fourteen," he announced. "It's the wind. Wind makes cold air feel colder, and that's what the wind chill number means. I tested it and everything." She laughed and handed him a second hat. "Then you'd better cover those ears, scientist." Noah pulled the hat down to his chin, grabbed the sled, and flung the door open. "Come on, Biscuit," he called into the wind. "We're riding in the wind chill!"

The spelling bee had taken over the reading room of the public library, where the long tables usually held newspapers and old men doing crossword puzzles. Rose sat in the front row of folding chairs with fourteen other spellers, her number pinned to her shirt. She had studied all week, categorizing her word list by language of origin, because knowing where a word came from helped her guess at letters she could not see.

Her first two words were easy. "Cinnamon." "Orchestra." She said each one slowly, picturing the letters on the library's return desk the way her grandmother had taught her, like stamps pressed into paper. The other spellers kept missing words, one by one, until only Rose and a boy named Dev from the middle school across town were left.

Dev got "penguin" and spelled it correctly. Then the judge, a librarian named Mrs. Okafor, looked at her card and said, "Vessel."

Rose started confidently. "V. E." In the quiet of the room she could hear the clock above the biography section ticking, and somewhere behind her a page turning. Then the picture in her mind wavered. Was it vessel with two s's, like a ship's tall sails, or one s, like the plain drinking cups at the water fountain? She had said one s. She believed it was two.

"Wait," she said. "Two s's. V, E, S, S, E, L. Vessel."

She looked up, hoping her restart had fixed it. Mrs. Okafor shook her head, gently, the way you might tell someone their shoelace had come undone too late. "I'm sorry, Rose. Starting over is allowed, but changing letters you've already said counts as a misspelling. That's the rule we use, the same as the Scripps National Spelling Bee." A little bell on the judge's table gave a soft ding, and Dev's mouth opened in surprise, as if he hadn't known the rule either.

Rose walked back to her seat through the smell of old paper and lemon polish. It felt unfair for a moment, even arbitrary, a rule that punished you for fixing your own mistake out loud. But she turned it over in her mind the way she turned over tricky words. The rule was not about being perfect the first time. It was about the letters you chose becoming real the moment you said them, spoken and done, like ink drying.

Dev won with "avocado." Afterward, while the chairs were being stacked, he came over to where Rose was pulling on her jacket. "I didn't know that rule," he admitted. "I would have done the same thing."

"There's a bee at the county building in March," Rose said. She zipped her jacket to the chin. "I'm going to practice out loud, all the way through, every single word."

Oliver leaned closer to the glowing laptop on the card table in Marcus's basement, where the smell of old carpet and popcorn filled the air. On the screen, a little orange cat stood on a green stage next to a number that read 0. "Watch," Marcus said. "Every time it touches the coin, the score goes up by one." He pressed the space bar, walked the cat into the coin, and the score jumped from 0 to 2. Then 5. Then 9. "That's not right," Oliver said, grabbing the popcorn bowl and sliding it aside so he could see better.

They stared at the blocks stacked in the script area. Oliver had come over specifically to learn this, because in two weeks the school coding club was holding a game showcase and he had promised to bring something playable. "Okay," he said slowly. "The score can't jump by itself. Something in the blocks is telling it to. It's happening too fast for us to see, so we have to figure out the hidden cause." He pointed at a gold if-then block. "What does this part do?"

"Checks if the cat is touching the coin," Marcus said. "And inside it, the score changes by one." Oliver tapped the screen where a purple forever loop wrapped around the if-then block like a ring around a smaller ring. "So the forever loop runs really fast, right? Maybe it runs so many times while the cat is still touching the coin that the score adds one over and over before the cat moves away." It was just a guess about something invisible, but it was testable. "Let's make it wait," Oliver said. He dragged a one-second wait block inside the if-then, under the score change. "Now we can actually see it happen."

Marcus pressed the space bar again. The cat touched the coin, and the score ticked up by one, once, then paused a full second before it could tick again. "One!" Oliver shouted, nearly knocking over his soda. "It's fixed! The cat was just standing there, and the loop kept firing." They high-fived so hard it stung. "Okay, now we integrate the sound," Marcus said, dragging in a block that played a chime whenever the score changed. "And we should make a durable version of the game for the showcase, in case the laptop gets bumped around." He pulled a scratched-up old laptop from under the stairs, the one Marcus called the conductor because it sat in the middle of everything and connected to the projector.

Upstairs the basement door opened, and Marcus's grandmother called down, "What are you two doing down there?" "Making a game!" Marcus yelled back. "It's called Scratch," Oliver said. "It came from the MIT Media Lab, and it first came out in 2007." She set down the cookies. "Blocks. Snapping like LEGO. I would have loved that."

Oliver grinned and copied the game onto a small drive, the version with the fixed score, the chime, and a rainbow trail behind the cat. He held the drive up to the light like it was made of gold. Carson stood beside his project board at the science fair and realized he had memorized the wrong thing. His whole display was about the periodic table, and he had drilled the names of thirty elements, but Judge Marlow from last year's fair was heading down the aisle, and last year she had asked questions nobody could answer. Priya leaned in from the next table, where her project on soil microbes sat under a hand-lettered sign reading PLEASE DO NOT LICK THE PETRI DISHES. "You look like your project just grew teeth," she said.

"I memorized names, not numbers. The judge asks about numbers." He pointed at the giant periodic table poster he'd glued to his board. Every box had a small number in the corner, and until that morning he had treated those numbers like decorations.

Priya squinted at the poster. "Wait. Look at the little numbers." She traced a finger across a row. "Six, seven, eight, nine. They count up by one, box after box. Down here too, eleven, twelve, thirteen. It goes all the way up in order." Carson checked the top corner of the poster. Hydrogen had a one. Helium had a two. In the corner of each box the numbers climbed, element by element, never jumping, never sliding backward. "That number is the atomic number," Priya said, reading the tiny label printed at the bottom of the poster. "And I bet it means protons."

"Protons," Carson repeated, and his stomach did something complicated. If the table ran in order of increasing atomic number, then every element had exactly one more proton than the one before it. Hydrogen carried one proton, helium two, lithium three, all the way down the line. He didn't need to memorize anything. He needed to count.

Judge Marlow stopped at his table. Behind her, a boy from the invasive plant project was frantly pulling kudzu vines off a teacher's wheeled cart, which was its own kind of science. She studied the poster. "Tell me," she said, "how many protons in oxygen?"

Carson ran his finger from hydrogen, one, two, three, past carbon and nitrogen, until he landed on oxygen. Eight elements along, eight protons. "Eight," he said, and then, because the gym was loud and he was tired of whispering, he said it louder. "Eight protons, because everything before it counts up by one."

Judge Marlow wrote something on her clipboard. Priya, from the next table, narrated in her best sports-announcer voice, "And the crowd goes mild."

The judge looked up, and for the first time in two years of science fairs, she smiled at Carson's poster.

story:
The wooden table at the back of the garage had belonged to the last tenant of the house, and it still smelled faintly of his pipe smoke. Ellie set her cutting board on it, then the pot, then the three onions her mother had handed her through the back door. Tonight was her turn to make dinner, and she had chosen soup: potatoes, carrots, broth, and onions sautéed until they turned glassy. Her little brother Theo trailed out behind her carrying the salt, because Theo wanted credit for the meal even though he mostly wanted to sprinkle things.

"Move your arm," Ellie said, and set the first onion on the board. The knife went through it with a soft crunch, and within seconds her eyes were stinging. She blinked, and then she was crying, actual tears sliding down her face while she stood in the calm evening light. Theo stared at her.

"Are you sad about the soup?" he asked.

"I'm not sad." She wiped her cheek with her wrist and kept chopping, and the tears kept coming, which felt absurd. She set the knife down and thought. Nothing was wrong with her eyes until the knife cut the onion. The onion had been whole and harmless sitting on the counter for two days. So it had to be the cutting itself. Something inside the onion was being let loose when the blade went through it, some invisible thing that floated up and found her eyes. She held the cut half an arm's length away and leaned back, and the stinging eased. When she leaned in over the board again, her eyes flooded.

"See, it's a gas or something," she said, chopping with her head tipped back, which looked ridiculous but worked. "Cutting it lets it out, and it gets to your eyes. That's the whole trick."

Theo shook his head slowly. "Onions can't attack you. You're so gullible."

"Put your face over the board, then."

He did, to prove her wrong, and lasted four seconds before his eyes streamed and he backed away, laughing and swiping at his face. "Okay, okay, it's true, it's true!" He grabbed the garden hose and dabbed his wet cheeks with cold water from his cupped hands, then went to sit on the step and draw in his notebook. He said he would depict the soup in a picture so he could prove he helped.

Ellie finished the onions, wiped her eyes dry, and carried the board to the pot. The pieces hissed when they hit the oil. Theo held up his drawing, a steaming bowl with a fierce onion wearing a frown.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
story:
Piper sat on the edge of the sandbox with her left arm propped in her lap, the new orange cast still smelling faintly like a wet chalkboard. She had chosen orange because purple was what everyone chose, and because orange was the color of the jump she should never have attempted. Two weeks ago she had launched off the top of the climbing dome, arms out like a superhero, and her classmates had watched her land wrong. Reckless, her grandmother had called it at the hospital, though she said it softly, like she was remembering her own broken collarbone from 1974.

The swing chains squeaked. Around her, kids ran the four-square court, and Marisol plopped down beside her, tracing the signatures on the cast with one finger. "Okay but a serious question," Marisol said. "What did people do before casts existed? Did they just walk around with floppy arms forever?"

"Armies," said Devon, arriving with his sandwich half-eaten. "I read it for my report. Broken bones everywhere."

Piper turned that over. Soldiers got hurt far from hospitals, so whoever fixed them needed something that hardened fast and could travel. She remembered the pamphlet rack beside the cast room, the paper she had read while waiting for the doctor, mostly because she had nothing else to do with one working hand. "It was a Dutch army surgeon," she said slowly, testing the memory. "Antonius Mathijsen. He came up with the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones. Plaster of Paris, like, the powder stuff. He published his method in 1852."

"Wait, is that in France?" Devon asked. "Plaster of Paris?"

"The powder got its name from Paris, but he was Dutch," Piper said. "Believe me, I read that paper four hundred times."

Marisol drummed her fingers on the cast. "So before 1852, what, nothing?"

That was the question Piper couldn't answer from memory, and it bothered her like a pebble in her shoe. She got up, trudged across the wood chips to the far fence where Mr. Okafor supervised recess, and asked him outright. He laughed. "Splints and hope, mostly. Sticks, cloth, whatever kept things still." Not everything had a neat answer. She filed that away and walked back.

"Verdict?" Marisol called.

"It holds up," Piper said. She held out her cast for the two of them to examine, turning it in the sunlight like a judge showing evidence to a jury. "So if I time traveled, I could still get a real cast. As long as it was after 1852." Then, quieter, looking at the climbing dome: "Whether I'd deserve one is a different question."

Marisol uncapped her marker and wrote her name right over the orange. "Next jump, land on your feet."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
story:
Ava slid The Scarlet Ibis across the library table like it might bite. "Mrs. Petty wants us to find foreshadowing," she told her friend Milo, who was balancing a pencil on his upper lip. "In a story this short. That's like hiding an elephant in a lunchbox."

"Just read it and look for weird stuff," Milo said, and the pencil fell off with a small clatter. "Weird stuff usually means something."

Weird stuff arrived on page three. A red bird blew in with a storm, exhausted, and dropped dead in the family's garden. Ava read the paragraph twice. "A scarlet ibis," she said. "It says it's a tropical bird, way off course. That is genuinely bizarre." She tapped the page. "Why would James Hurst, in 1960, spend a whole page on a bird funeral unless the bird mattered?"

"Maybe he likes birds," said Milo. "Some people are bird people."

Ava had a different idea, and she wanted to test it before she trusted it. In the margin of her notes she wrote: red bird = Doodle? Doodle was the little brother in the story, fragile and frail, born weak, the one everybody worried about. If the two of them corresponded, then the bird dying in the garden wasn't just sad, it was a message about what was coming for Doodle. Her test was simple. If the bird was foreshadowing, the story should keep linking them, and the storm should come back.

She read with her finger under the line, and there it was: the red bird, and Doodle, both worn out, both out of place, both struggling to survive. Then, near the end, the narrator left Doodle behind in a storm, and Ava felt her stomach drop, because she already knew. She flipped the page with one eye half closed, the way you check a bruise after a possible concussion in gym class, braced for the worst. Doodle was dead, and he was red, like the bird.

"HA," Ava said, a little too loud. The librarian raised one finger without looking up.

"Ha, what?" Milo leaned over. He'd been drawing a dinosaur in his notes, which was his version of research.

"The bird. It was foreshadowing the whole time. The storm, the red, the garden. I called it in my margin, page three, timestamped in pencil."

"That's creepy," Milo said, impressed. "You predicted a fictional death from a fictional bird."

"It's not creepy, it's symbolism," said Ava, and copied her margin note onto her worksheet in her neatest handwriting, the kind with the perfect loops. Under Evidence she wrote the bird, the storm, the garden. Under Prediction, one word: Doodle. Then she slid the paper toward Milo. "Okay, hotshot. Find me a symbol in your dinosaur."

Milo studied it. "The dinosaur is green," he said slowly. "Green corresponds with my jealousy of your worksheet."

Ava threw her eraser at him.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
story:
Chase had seventy-one cents in his pocket, a stack of lemonade receipts in his backpack, and one big question: how much money had he actually made this summer? He counted the crumpled dollars and sticky nickels twice at the kitchen table and got two different answers, so on Saturday morning he carried the whole mess to the public library and signed up for the computer lab.

"Spreadsheet club starts at ten," said the librarian, Ms. Okafor, sliding a flyer across the desk. "Bring your own numbers if you've got them."

He had numbers, all right. Forty-two days of lemonade, written on napkins, in a notebook, and once on his own arm.

The lab had six computers and two other kids, plus an old man in a cardigan who had set up a thermos like he planned to stay until closing. Chase chose the seat next to him, mostly because the man's screen already showed a neat grid of boxes.

"That's a spreadsheet," the man said. "You type numbers in the cells, and it does the arithmetic for you." He leaned over. "What are you working on?"

"Lemonade empire," Chase said. "But I don't trust my adding. Last week I thought I made nine dollars and it was really six."

The man laughed so hard he sloshed his coffee. "Then you've come to the right place. In 1979 I was about your age, and my father brought home an Apple II with VisiCalc on it. VisiCalc was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers. My father didn't write it himself, of course. It was written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston. He'd sit there for hours, adding up columns, saying he'd never have to balance his checkbook by hand again."

Chase stared at him. "They had spreadsheets before I was born?"

"Before I had gray hair," the man said, which struck Chase as an even more impressive span of time.

Ms. Okafor gathered everyone around the projector. "Today, a formula that adds a whole column, and a bar chart. Type equals, then SUM, then open parenthesis." Chase typed carefully, and when he pressed Enter, the total appeared like magic: $84.35. He checked it against his notebook, then against the napkins, and all three agreed, which had never once happened before.

But something bothered him. His daily sales looked wildly different, from fifty cents to seven dollars, and he couldn't see why. Rainy days were bad, sure, but Tuesday had been sunny and he'd sold almost nothing. He sorted the rows and studied them until he spotted it: every slow day, the rec center pool was closed, and the swimmers who usually trudged past his stand had never come by. It was a hidden cause, invisible on the napkins, but sitting right there in the pattern once he made a chart. The tall bars and short bars told the story better than his memory ever had.

"Grandpa," called a girl across the room, "you promised you'd help me with mine." The old man pushed back his chair, then paused at Chase's screen.

"You found something," he said.

"The pool," Chase said. "Closed Tuesdays. My chart knows things I didn't."

The man smiled at the bars like they were old friends. "That's what my father used to say about VisiCalc. It remembered so he didn't have to." Then he went to help his granddaughter, and Chase pulled out a fresh napkin to plan next summer's stand.

He was going to sell exactly nothing on Tuesdays, and he was going to sell it brilliantly somewhere else.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
story:
The computer lab smelled like warm plastic and thirty kids who had all had gym before lunch. Isla had exactly one class period to finish her bake-sale report, because Ms. Petra had announced that whoever turned in a spreadsheet with a working total and a chart would inherit the job of treasurer for the whole spring fundraiser. Isla wanted that job. She had already imagined announcing, at the audition for next year's student council, that she managed money for a real organization. It sounded credible, and being treasurer of bake sales was a start.

She had typed the cookie sales into column C, rows two through seven, and now she needed the sum. There was a formula bar at the top, and she knew it started with an equals sign, but she could not remember what went inside. Her friend Priya had done this in last period's class. Isla pulled out her phone under the desk and texted, then called, keeping her voice at a whisper. "Just tell me the formula you used."

"You type equals, then SUM, then the first cell and the last cell with a colon," Priya said. "Like equals SUM, C4, colon, C9." Isla typed it. The total came out as 4.75. Her column held numbers like 42 and 18. A total of 4.75 was not a total of anything.

"Read me the exact cells again," she said. "Slowly."

"C4, colon, C9. I'm literally reading it off my paper." Isla looked at her screen. C4, she saw, was not the top of her column. The top of her column was C2, because her numbers started in row two. The 4.75, when she clicked it, came from a single cell, the one in row four, which held the price of one cupcake. That gave her an idea about how the addresses worked, and she tested it right there. She clicked C7, and the box at the top of the screen read C7, and sure enough, that cell sat in column C, row seven. The letter was the column, the number was the row. So a cell's address was its column letter first, then its row number, and C4 meant column C, row 4, not row C, column 4. Priya had read it backwards off her paper, or copied it backwards, or both.

Isla fixed the formula to say C2, colon C7, and the total appeared: 156.50. She selected the column, clicked the chart button, and a bar chart sprang up with six bars, the tall one for brownies lording it over the short one for lemon squares. Priya was still talking on the phone. "Is it right? Did it work?"

Isla saved the file, twice, and pulled the flash drive from the port. "You owe me a cookie," she said.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
story:
The envelope sat in Tyler's backpack all morning, and on the bus he finally opened it under his seat so nobody would crowd him. Inside was the phone his parents had promised, plus a note in his mom's handwriting: "Bus and home only. No school use. We permit one hour a day, and we can see the report." Tyler slid the phone out. It weighed almost nothing, lighter than the granola bar in his pocket.

Last night his grandfather had held the same phone at the kitchen table and laughed. "You know the first handheld cell phone call ever made? Martin Cooper made it, and that phone weighed about 1.1 kilograms. Two and a half pounds, Tyler. Like carrying a bag of sugar glued to your ear." Tyler had laughed too, but now, on the bumpy bus, he wondered if his grandfather was exaggerating the way he exaggerated about walking ten miles to school in the snow.

Marcus dropped into the seat beside him and peered over. "That's it? The famous phone?" He grabbed Tyler's math textbook and hefted it in one hand. "This is probably close to two and a half pounds." Tyler took the book, then the phone, one in each hand, balancing them like a scale. The book pulled his hand down hard. The phone floated. His grandfather had told the truth, and for once Tyler had checked instead of just believing him, which felt different and better.

But there was still the note, and the report his parents could see. Tyler knew that Marcus had become notorious for running up data charges last year, and that Tyler's cousin in Britain kept complaining that the monarchy got better phone plans than regular people, whatever that meant. Tyler didn't want to end up on either list. He remembered that the bus had no Wi-Fi, so anything he downloaded here would eat data, which had to be what had burned through Marcus's plan. He tested it: he turned the phone's data off, then tried to load a video. Nothing moved. He turned data back on and the video started. So that was the hidden switch, the thing he couldn't see but could now prove.

"Watch," Tyler said, and turned the data off again, this time leaving it off. He opened the note app instead and typed, "Ask Grandpa more about Martin Cooper." The bus swayed around the long curve by the pond, and the phone rode weightless in his palm, hardly there at all.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
story:
Colton had one hour before the bus left, and one worksheet with a blank half page: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. He stood in the museum's frontier room, where a glass case held a leather diary no bigger than his hand, opened to a page of faded brown ink.

His first instinct was to grab his phone and copy a summary from the internet, but the worksheet said primary source, and his teacher had circled those words twice. So he leaned over the case and read the neat, cramped handwriting of a settler named Amos Reed. The docent, a college student named Priya, unlocked a drawer of reproduction pages so visitors could handle copies, and Colton took the stack to a bench and started reading in a systematic way, page by page, first line to last.

The early pages were what he expected. Amos wrote about poor soil back east, about cheap land in Oregon, about a wagon and oxen and his wife Ruth's cold hands. Then Colton hit a page dated March 1848, and the handwriting changed. It grew jagged, the words crowded together. "Word has come of gold at Sutter's Mill in California," Amos had written, "found this January past. Every man on the trail talks of it. Ruth says we go to Oregon for the farm, but I confess my heart pounds otherwise."

Colton sat back. He'd assumed everyone in a covered wagon wanted farmland, the picture from every textbook he'd ever seen. But the diary said something else. Amos had started out for land, and then gold was discovered, in January 1848, and that discovery started what the trail travelers were already calling the gold rush, people heading west in huge numbers just for that. Some travelers came for money, not farmland. That was the hidden thing, sitting under the story he thought he knew. To test it, he flipped forward through the pages, looking for one change he could trace. He found it: after March, Amos stopped writing about soil. He wrote about rivers, pans, and a claim.

He raised his hand and waved Priya over. "So the gold rush pulled people west?" he asked. "It wasn't just farms?"

Priya nodded at the page. "The California Gold Rush," she said. "That's what they called it."

Colton filled the blank half of his worksheet in careful print, quoting the March entry, then wrote his own sentence underneath: the discovery at Sutter's Mill in January 1848 changed why people like Amos moved west, because a primary source can show a reason that changed mid-journey. On the last page of the stack, in ink gone thin and pale, Amos had written a single line from Sacramento. Colton read it twice, then copied it onto the corner of his worksheet so he wouldn't lose it: "Ruth was right about the farm, but I was right about the gold, and I am sorry for both."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
story:
The outdoor track circled the basketball court at Riverside Park, so Ethan could practice running while his older cousin Marcus shot free throws on the blacktop inside the loop. Coach Reyes had assigned Ethan his first eight hundred metre race on Saturday, and Ethan wanted it badly, because the winner of the city meet got to carry the team banner at the season parade. The problem was the distance itself. His watch said he always started fast, died halfway, and finished crawling.

Marcus waved him over between shots. "You know it's only two laps, right? Four hundred metre track, so the eight hundred is exactly two laps. Everybody plans it as a first lap and a second lap."

"Two laps," Ethan repeated. "That's all?" He had assumed it was some enormous distance, and now a new worry replaced the old one. If the race was only two laps, then the thing that separated winners from losers was invisible. Nobody could see energy being saved or spent. He would have to deduce it from numbers, from the way his legs felt at each mark, like a detective working with clues he could not watch directly.

He decided on an experiment. He did a time trial, and at the halfway line he counted the runners scattered around the loop, a quick census of who was ahead and who was behind, and matched it against where his own legs were burning. He tried again the next evening, holding back on purpose through the whole first lap even though it felt embarrassingly slow, then letting everything go on the second. His total time dropped by six seconds. Same legs, same track, different plan. He grinned at Marcus, who was dribbling with one hand and watching with the other.

On race day, the starter's gun cracked and twenty boys surged forward. Ethan stayed near the back, and the crowd at the far turn began shouting at the leaders, voices rising as runners stretched out. Rounding into the home straight, the boy beside him, wearing an eccentric mismatched pair of shoes, one red and one green, suddenly sprinted as if the finish had come. Ethan's own legs screamed at him to follow. For three strides he almost did, because everyone was yelling and the finish line flag was right there, snapping in the wind. Then his experiment spoke louder than the crowd. One lap down. One to go.

The red-and-green shoe boy crossed the line, slowed, and staggered when he realized nobody else had stopped. Ethan passed him on the backstretch of the second lap, breathing in rhythm, and poured out everything he had saved as the flag came around again. He lunged across the line second, and Marcus was already vaulting the railing, shouting, "That's my cousin!"

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
story:
Payton sat cross-legged on Grandma Ruth's kitchen floor with a laptop balanced on a stack of old cookbooks, because the table was crowded with jars of damson jam. She had promised her cousin Marcus she would text him a prime-checker program before his math club meeting on Thursday, and it was already Tuesday. The kitchen smelled of sugar and scorched fruit, and Grandma Ruth moved between the stove and the counter like a diplomat negotiating between two bubbling pots, warning each one not to boil over.

Payton typed her loop: for every number from 2 up to the one the user typed, check whether it divides evenly. If none of them do, the number is prime. She tested it with 7, and the screen printed "prime." She tried 9, and it printed "not prime," which was right, since 9 divides by 3. She exhaled, feeling the program finally taking shape after two evenings of nothing but error messages.

Then she tested 2, because Marcus would surely try it. The screen said "not prime." Payton frowned at it. Her loop started checking at 2, so of course 2 divided evenly by 2, and the program stamped it not prime, which had to be wrong. She flipped through her notes, then stared at the counter, where Grandma Ruth was wiping up a sticky ring of spilled syrup. "Two has to count," Payton said out loud. "There's nothing smaller to divide it except 1, and 1 doesn't count."

Grandma Ruth peered over her shoulder at the screen. "I remember your grandfather going on about that," she said. "Two is the only even prime number." Payton blinked. She hadn't thought about even and odd at all. She scribbled on a napkin: 4, 6, 8, 10. Every larger even number could be divided evenly by 2, so none of them could ever be prime. Two was the only one that slipped through, the loner in the even crowd. That was the pattern her program had to honor.

She changed one line, telling the program to answer "prime" for 2 before the loop even began. Then she typed test after test: 2, 3, 4, 11, 25, 100. Each answer came back correct, the successes cumulative now, one built on the last. Her fingers were sticky from the jam jar Grandma Ruth had set beside her, but she typed the final message to Marcus anyway: "Done. It even handles 2. Try to break it."

Marcus texted back a minute later: "2 is prime. You fixed the tricky one." Payton grinned and closed the laptop, and Grandma Ruth slid a warm scone onto the cookbook stack beside her.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
story:
Annabelle crouched at the top of the skate park's shallow bowl with a marble, a stopwatch, and a clipboard, because Mr. Ruiz had said their graphs were due tomorrow and hers was still blank. She had tried measuring the marble in the school hallway, but kids kept walking through, and her graph had come out a mess of dots that jumped around like flies. Here, on the smooth concrete of the bowl's rim, nobody would bother her.

"Whatcha doing?" A boy on a skateboard rolled up beside her, one wheel squeaking. His name was Dev, and he'd been circling the park all afternoon, waiting for his turn on the big ramp.

"Timing a ball," Annabelle said. "Ten centimeters, twenty, thirty. I write down how long it takes to reach each mark, then I plot it."

Dev scratched his chin. "You can draw a picture of speed?"

"That's the weird part. You can't see speed. You only see where the ball is and what the clock says. The graph is how you catch it." She let the marble go and clicked the stopwatch as it crossed each chalk mark. "Five seconds. Almost the same again. Almost the same again."

Dev sat down on his board, forgetting the ramp entirely. "It's slowing down, though, right? Everything slows down. My grandpa says his pension slows down every year, whatever that means. Money stuff."

"The marble loses a little speed, sure. But look." She plotted her points on the clipboard: ten centimeters at five seconds, twenty at ten, thirty at fifteen. When she connected them with her ruler, they fell along one clean line, slanting up from the corner like a hill. "It's straight."

"So?"

"So I thought the line would curve. A ball that's slowing should bend the line, shouldn't it?" She stared at it. The floor was so smooth, so polished by ten years of skateboards, that the marble barely lost anything at all. She dropped her pencil and grabbed the marble again. "Okay, one more run to justify this. If it's real, it'll do it twice."

She rolled the marble down the far side of the bowl, where the concrete was rougher and scattered with pebbles. This time the dots scattered, and the line she could draw through them bent and drooped. She held both graphs side by side.

"Dev, look. A straight sloping line means the ball is going at a constant speed. This one's straight, so it's constant. This one bends, so it isn't."

Dev picked up the marble and squinted through it at the sun. "So on the smooth floor, the ball never changes its mind."

"Something like that," Annabelle said. She checked her watch and yelped, because the park closed at six and her graph still needed labels. She flipped to a clean page and started the axes, and Dev, still holding her marble hostage, said, "Do the rough floor one more time. I want to watch it bend."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Eleanor had the whole evening planned: roast chicken, a big green salad, and her grandmother's lemon cake. Her parents were both working late, and she wanted dinner ready when they walked in the door. She'd already trimmed the raw chicken and set it in the oven pan, and now she pulled the lettuce from the fridge and reached for the cutting board on the counter, the one still slick from the chicken.

She stopped with the knife in her hand. Something her science teacher had said in the fall came back to her, something about bacteria hopping from one food to another. It even had a name. "Cross-contamination," she said out loud, trying the word. The lettuce was going into the salad raw. Nobody would cook it, and cooking was what made the chicken safe in the first place. The lettuce would go straight from board to bowl to mouths, exactly as it was.

She rinsed the knife, washed her hands, and slid the used board into the sink. Then she pulled the plastic-wrapped clean board from the cabinet, the one she used for bread, and set it on the counter beside the salad bowl. Outside the window the sky had turned an ominous gray, and fat drops of precipitation spattered the glass. If it kept up, her dad would come home soaked, which meant she should put towels by the front door too. She added it to her mental list while she tore the lettuce into pieces.

Her little brother Marcus wandered in, sniffing the air. "Is that cake?" He pointed at the lemon zesting setup next to the stove.

"Cake comes after dinner," Eleanor said. "Want a job? Wash these tomatoes." She handed him three and elaborated on the plan, since Marcus always worked better when he knew the whole shape of it. "Salad first, then chicken comes out, then we ice the cake while everything's hot on plates."

"What's this board for?" Marcus asked, picking up the second one from the sink.

"That one had raw chicken on it," Eleanor said. "It has to be washed with soap before anything else touches it."

Marcus made a face and set it down like it might bite him. "That's why you got the other one out?"

"Exactly." She dried her hands and checked the oven. Through the little window the chicken was already turning golden at the edges.

When their parents came in, shaking rain off their coats, the salad was sitting crisp and cold on the table, and Marcus was carrying the lemon cake with both hands like a trophy. Their mother paused at the counter, taking in the clean board, the soapy one in the rack, the two of them standing there.

"You used different boards," she said.

Eleanor smiled and lifted the carving knife. "Dinner in ten minutes."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
story:
Victor stood at the microphone in the school gymnasium with his hands jammed in his pockets, waiting for the word he was sure would end his run at the county spelling bee. Across the bleachers sat his little sister, holding the flashcards he had made her carry on the bus even though she complained the whole way.

"Bite," the pronouncer said. "B-I-T-E. The silent e does nothing. This language is a mess," Victor whispered, because the pronouncer had already called time on the word before, when Victor had stopped mid-spell to grumble about it, and the judges had agreed to postpone his turn until the end of the round rather than mark him out.

From the bleachers his sister shouted, "Mrs. Okoye called it the Great Vowel Shift!" Victor's face went hot, but the judges only chuckled, and the pronouncer nodded. "That's true," she said. "Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed after spellings had started to become fixed." She tapped her cards. "It's a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation. Now spell the word, please."

Victor had planned to argue that the whole system was rigged, that memorizing was like being frugal with the wrong currency, saving up letters that bought nothing. But something clicked instead. If the vowels had shifted while the letters stayed frozen, then the e in bite wasn't a trick. It was a fossil, proof of an older sound. He tested the idea quickly, silently. "Meet" must once have rhymed with "mate." "Bite" with "beet." The pattern held, at least for the words in his stack of flashcards, which he had drilled like a frontiersman chopping through a wall of vowels nobody had warned him about. Spelling wasn't random. It was archaeology.

"B-I-T-E," he said. "Bite." The bell stayed silent, and the pronouncer smiled and gave the next speller a word, and Victor walked back to the folding chair in the line of surviving contestants. His sister gave him two thumbs up. He had come in believing the bee was pure memorization, a contest of brute repetition, and now he wasn't so sure. There was a system underneath, buried but real, and he wanted to dig for it.

He slid the flashcards out of his back pocket and, on the bus ride home, turned them over one by one, hunting for fossils. When he found "name," he tapped the card against the window and said, "You too, huh."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
story:
Luca had carried four bean plants into the gymnasium in a cardboard box, and now he stood beside his folding table arranging them in a row. Three of the plants had grown tall under his grow light at home, but one was small and pale. That one was his favorite, even though kids walking past kept frowning at it.

"Your plant's dying," said Marcus, leaning over the table. "That's going to embarrass you when the judges come."

"That one's the one that got only plain water," Luca said. "The other three got the fertilizer. It's my control group."

Marcus looked blank, so Luca pointed at each pot in turn. "This one got fertilizer once a week. This one got it twice. This one got it every day. And the control group gets no change at all, no fertilizer, just water. That way I can compare everything against it." The plain-water plant had barely grown, while the once-a-week plant had shot up taller than the others. The every-day plant had yellow leaves that looked almost endangered, drooping at the tips. Luca wrote a note on his chart about it.

During the fair, a judge in a green sweater stopped at Luca's table. She asked what the small plant was for, and Luca explained his rows and his chart, showing how the once-a-week plant had grown the most while the plain-water plant gave him the starting point to measure from. The judge asked what he would do differently next time, and Luca said he would test more plants in each group, because one bean plant alone could just be a weird bean plant. The judge smiled at that and made a mark on her clipboard.

After she moved on, Marcus came back with his own project, a volcano that had fizzled twice before working. "I just dumped baking soda in all my test cups," he admitted. "I didn't have anything to compare against."

"You could run it again," Luca said. "Set one cup aside with nothing in it at all. My mom says the second try is where the real science happens." He slid his chart across the table so Marcus could see the rows.

Marcus studied it, then jogged off toward the supply table where the extra cups were stacked. "I'm redoing it before the next judge comes around!" he called back.

Luca turned his plain-water plant so its label faced the aisle, right beside the tall one.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
story:
Blake had one hundred eighty-two dollars in his desk drawer, and he wanted it to be more. It sat under a model rocket kit he had never built, and every so often he counted it, which changed nothing.

At dinner his sister Priya, who was sixteen and annoyingly good with money, mentioned that her savings account earned six percent interest. Blake slid his oatmeal-raisin cookies toward her until she agreed to explain. Simple interest, she said, paid you the same dollars every year, six dollars on every hundred, over and over. She drew it on a napkin: a flat line of identical payments, five years, thirty dollars on a hundred. Then she said the magic word, compound, and drew the line bending upward, because with compound interest you earned interest on your interest. Blake squinted at the napkin until the numbers blurred.

"Both are six percent," he said slowly, "but one of them keeps feeding itself."

Priya shrugged, which was how she confessed she had already known this for two years and never told him.

That night he sat at the kitchen table with a calculator, graph paper, and the last of the milk. He worked out five years both ways. Simple gave a hundred dollars thirty more dollars. Compound gave more than that, and the difference was small, which disappointed him until he noticed the gap between the lines growing wider each year, like two runners where one kept speeding up. He could not see the interest itself, nothing you could hold, but the pattern on his paper proved something invisible was happening. He tested it backward, too: he started with the compound total and peeled off six percent five times, and landed back near a hundred, close enough that the little difference had to be the interest on interest stacking up.

"How long until my money doubles?" he asked Priya from the doorway.

"Rule of seventy-two," she called back, halfway asleep. "Divide seventy-two by the yearly percentage rate."

He did the math on his hand. Seventy-two divided by six was twelve years. Twelve years at six percent, so his two hundred birthday checks would become four hundred by the time he was twenty-five. He wrote the number on the napkin and taped it inside his desk drawer, right on top of the rocket kit.

The next morning he found the drawer open and forty dollars missing, replaced by a note in Priya's handwriting: "Loan. Compound interest applies. Six percent, payable in cookies."

Blake counted what remained, then counted it again. "Twelve years to double," he muttered, "but about two weeks to get even." He headed for the kitchen to bake.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
The highway unrolled ahead of them like a ribbon left in the sun, and George had the whole back seat to himself, which almost made up for nine hours of driving. His science teacher had handed out a packet before spring break: rainfall and temperature graphs for two places, one a rainforest station beside an estuary on the coast, the other a stretch of desert they were, at this very moment, driving through. George's assignment was to compare the climates. His dad had promised they'd stop at the visitor center outside town, and George wanted to be ready, because his older sister Kayla had made a bet with him back in February. She'd said he couldn't figure out what made a desert a desert. He'd said deserts were hot, obviously. She'd grinned in that infuriating way and told him to look it up.

He looked it up now, phone balanced on his knee while saguaro cactuses slid past the window, their arms raised like people hailing a bus. Less than about 250 millimeters of rain a year. He said it out loud, then again, quieter. Ten inches. He pulled out the rainfall graph for the rainforest station and traced the bars with one finger, month after month, some of them taller than his thumb. Then he checked the temperature line, which never dropped below warm. When he flipped to the desert graph, the bars were stubs, hardly bumps at all, though the temperature line swung wildly between baking days and shivering nights.

"A desert is a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters of rain a year," he said to Kayla. "Ten inches. That's the rule."

"So what?" she said, not looking up from her music.

"So it doesn't say anything about temperature. It only says rain." He tapped the packet. "Which means a cold place could count too. A snowy place, even."

Kayla pulled out one earbud. "No way."

"Way. If it gets less than ten inches of precipitation, it's a desert, even if it snows." He remembered, suddenly, choosing his answer back in February, blurting out "hot" without thinking, and he could still feel how dumb it had seemed later, lying awake in his bunk bed. He'd wanted to guess fast instead of guessing right. He wasn't sure yet whether the bet counted as won, since he'd been wrong first, and Kayla would absolutely argue that it didn't.

At the visitor center, a wall map showed rainfall totals painted in bands of color, and George stood in front of it while a lizard watched him from a rock outside the glass. He found a gray stretch far to the south, marked with snowflake symbols, and below it a number: 180 millimeters. Kayla leaned in beside him, silent for a long moment.

"Okay," she said at last. "Half a win."
